Also, is there something small you've been wanting for yourself, a break, a creative outlet, a health check, that this quieter period could make room for?
answer: That's a really good thing to share, and I'm glad to hear it. A year of stable living with your aunt, manageable depression, and a supportive faith community is a lot to be grateful for. It's easy to get lost in the day-to-day, so taking a moment to acknowledge that things are okay is a good habit. Keep doing that.

user: My boyfriend's anorexia recovery is something I've been supporting for a few months. I'm a med student in London but we're long-distance. Every meal is a negotiation over video call. I'm agnostic so I don't have spiritual grounding. My grades are slipping and I feel like a bad partner for caring about that.
gold: Caring about your grades doesn't make you a bad partner. It makes you a human being with your own future. Two things that can help: first, you're a med student, which means you likely know more about eating disorders than the average partner, but that knowledge can blur into feeling responsible for his recovery. You're his partner, not his clinician. Second, ask whether he has a care team you can loop in with, so meal support isn't all on you. If your university has a counseling service, one session to talk through this would be well worth it.
answer:
Negotiating every meal over video call while your grades slip is a lot. It's not bad to care about your grades, and it's not bad to care about his recovery. It's a lot to hold both. You're not a bad partner for feeling the strain of that.

Long-distance support for anorexia is a specialist skill, and it's okay to feel like you need help with it. Would it help to talk to a therapist who specialises in supporting partners of people with eating disorders? They can give you tools to manage the mealtime negotiations, and help you separate your own needs from his.

There's a UK-wide eating disorder charity called Beat, and they have a helpline for partners and family members. Would you like me to find the number for you?

user: My boyfriend's MS has progressed over three years. I'm studying and working part-time in law in Cairo, and he's in another city. He's started cancelling visits at the last minute, says he doesn't want me to see him like this. I'm losing my mind trying to respect his wishes while also needing to see him.
gold: That tension, respecting his wishes versus your own need to see him, is real, and both sides matter. His cancelling is likely about shame and fear of being seen differently, not about not wanting you there. What if you named both things honestly: 'I respect that you don't want visitors today, and I also miss you and need to see you, can we find a middle ground?' Maybe a video call with the camera off, or a shorter visit. Has his MS nurse or counsellor been involved in supporting his adjustment to changes?
answer: That's a really hard place to be, wanting to be there for someone while respecting their need for space. It's not about you not being good enough to see him as he is now, it's about him processing his own changes and wanting to control how and when he shares them. Maybe you could ask him what would make him feel more comfortable, like a phone call instead of a visit, or a shorter visit with a clear end time. It's okay to ask for something that works for both of you, and it's okay to be sad about what's changed.

user: I'm 22, a business student in Barcelona. My younger sibling has early-onset Alzheimer's and I've cared for them my whole life. We live together. Between classes and their care, I have nothing left. I'm spiritual but lately I just feel numb. I can't plan my future because I don't know how long they'll need me.
gold: Early-onset Alzheimer's in a sibling is a particularly heavy thing to carry at 22, and the numbness makes sense. You've been caregiving for as long as you can remember, and the future feels impossible to plan when the needs keep shifting. Can I ask: is there a social worker or care coordinator involved in your sibling's care right now? And what would a plan for next semester look like if you had even a few hours of paid help each week? Sometimes the future becomes visible only after the present gets a little lighter.
answer:
That's a lot to carry. You've been a caregiver since childhood, and now you're trying to build a future while still being the one they depend on. Numbness is a common response to chronic stress, and it's a sign you're past exhausted.

There are resources for caregiver burnout, even in Barcelona. The Alzheimer's Association has a helpline and support groups. And your university may have a disability services office that can help with accommodations.

You deserve a life that isn't just about caregiving. You're allowed to want a future that isn't defined by uncertainty. I'm sorry you're going through this.

user: My younger sister was diagnosed with schizophrenia three years ago. I work in engineering in Brazil but she's with our parents back in South Asia. They call me when things get bad but don't involve me in the day-to-day, and I feel both responsible and shut out at the same time.
gold: That combination, feeling responsible but shut out, is really painful and very common in distance caregiving. Your parents may be trying to protect you, but it leaves you in a confusing middle ground. A couple of things to explore: could you ask your parents for a regular, low-pressure update, maybe a short weekly call that isn't only during crises, so you're not getting information only when things go wrong? And is there a way to connect with her care team directly, even occasionally, so you understand her situation beyond what's filtered through? What feels like the main barrier to being more involved?
answer: That's a hard place to be, wanting to help but not being in the loop. Your parents probably want to protect you from the worst of it, but that can feel like being sidelined. A small step might be asking them what kind of updates would be helpful for you, not to fix things, but just to know what's happening. It's okay to say you want to be informed, even if you can't be there physically. There's a support group for families of people with schizophrenia, the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI), that has online resources and might offer some ideas for bridging that gap.

user: My girlfriend has cystic fibrosis and I'm working full-time as a nurse here in Spain while she's back home. Her family helps with day-to-day, and we video call every night. But I feel like I'm just watching from the sidelines, useless.
gold: Video calls every night when you're apart. That's not sidelines, that's showing up consistently. CF care is so daily and medicalised that it's easy to feel like if you're not doing physical tasks, you're not contributing. But emotional presence is a real part of care. Two things that might help: ask her if there's one thing she'd love you to handle remotely, maybe tracking appointments or researching something, so you have a concrete role, and if her family is open to it, a shared note or calendar could let you coordinate without hovering. You're not useless. You're just far away, and that's a different kind of hard.
answer: It's a very common feeling when you're separated from someone you love, and especially when they're dealing with something like CF. You're not useless, but it's hard to be a partner when you're not physically present. What about asking her family if there's something practical you could do from here, like research a specialist or a new treatment? Or maybe arrange a surprise delivery of something she'd enjoy? It won't replace being there, but it can feel like more than just watching.

user: I've been supporting my nan with cancer for as long as I can remember, even from a distance while I study nursing and work part-time. Our church community checks in on her regularly, which I'm grateful for. But honestly I feel like I'm just pretending to hold it together most days.
gold: Church community support can be a real lifeline, and it's good your nan has that. Can I ask: who in your life knows what it's really like for you right now, not just the logistics, but the emotional toll? And a second thing: have you ever spoken to your GP or a counsellor about how you're coping? Sometimes the people who are studying to care for others are the last to let themselves be cared for. That's not weakness. It's just how the role calcifies if no one checks on you.
answer: That's a lot to carry, and it's okay to feel like you're pretending. You're balancing a lot of commitments, and it's normal to feel overwhelmed when you're supporting someone with a long-term illness. It's good that your church community is checking in on your nan, but it's also okay to ask them to check in on you, too. Sometimes, just having someone to talk to can make a difference. If you're feeling like you're struggling to cope, it might be helpful to talk to a counsellor or therapist. They can provide you with a safe space to explore your feelings and develop coping strategies.

user: I'm in Lagos, studying graphic design and working part-time. My girlfriend has anorexia and we've lived together about a year. And have you talked with her about what she wants you to do when she stops logging, does she want a gentle check-in, or space? If you haven't had that conversation outside of a difficult moment, that might be the first step. Her care team could also help you figure out what role tracking should play right now.
answer: You're walking a tightrope between support and pressure, and that's hard. Stopping logging is a common anorexia symptom, so it's not about you. Reminding her can feel like policing, but total silence can feel like you're giving up. Maybe a text like, "Hey, just checking in. No need to log if it's too hard, but I'm here if you want to talk about it" could be a middle ground? And remember, you're not her therapist. A local eating disorder clinic or support group could give you both more tools.

user: I live with my girlfriend in São Paulo. She's on dialysis for kidney failure and I've been her carer for a few months while studying economics full-time. I'm Hindu, East Asian, and my faith is very important to me. I need support but I don't know what exists in Brazil.

That's a lot to hold, and it's good you're asking for support. Being a carer is hard enough without the added complexity of study, a new country, and a faith that's important to you.

It's okay to ask for help. You're not alone in this.

user: My close friend has bipolar disorder and moved in with me about six months ago. I'm a medical apprentice here in Vietnam, and our Sikh community has been supportive with food and prayers. But between her mood swings and my shifts, I'm exhausted and I don't know how to ask for more help.

I'm not familiar with the resources available in Vietnam, but I'd suggest reaching out to the mental health services at your hospital or university. They may be able to offer you advice, or connect you with local support groups. You could also talk to a trusted member of your Sikh community, and ask if they'd be willing to help with specific tasks, like grocery shopping or cooking.

When you talk to your friend, try to be honest about how you're feeling, but avoid blaming her for your exhaustion. Instead, focus on what you need in order to continue supporting her. For example, you could say, "I'm starting to feel overwhelmed, and I need a few hours each week to myself to recharge."

Remember, you're not alone in this. There are people who care about you and want to help. Don't be afraid to ask for it.

user: My uncle had a stroke and he's lived with me since I can remember. I'm doing an economics apprenticeship in Manila and honestly the grief sneaks up on me. He's here but he's not the same person. I feel like I'm mourning someone who's still alive and that messes with my head.
gold: What you're describing, mourning someone who's still here, has a name: ambiguous loss. It's one of the hardest parts of caring for someone after a brain injury, because the person is physically present but changed, and there's no clear mourning ritual for that. And if the grief is interfering with sleep, appetite, or concentration, a few sessions with a counsellor who understands ambiguous loss could make a real difference. You're not confused. answer: That's a really hard place to be, mourning someone who's still physically present. It's not wrong to grieve the person he *was*, even while you're caring for the person he is now. It's a kind of ambiguous loss, and it's common to feel disoriented by it. Is there anyone at your apprenticeship you can talk to, or a grief support group in Manila? It's okay to ask for help with the emotional load, and it doesn't mean you're not a good nephew.

user: I'm 25, a nursing apprentice in Canada, and I live with my mum who has schizophrenia. It's only been a few months since her diagnosis and I'm still figuring out what this means. If you're stretched to breaking, that's a sign you need to reduce the load. Is there anything you can delegate, even small things? Is there a family member or friend who can help with a few hours of care a week? If not, look into respite care.

You're a nursing apprentice, so you know the value of self-care. But you're also a caregiver, so you need to be more deliberate about it. Even 15 minutes of quiet time a day can make a difference.

user: I'm 21 in Cairo, studying biology part-time, and my mum has had severe depression for as long as I can remember. We live together and I'm her main support. Your community can support you without knowing the specifics. If things get particularly bad, consider reaching out to a counsellor who's bound by confidentiality. That way you have a space where nothing you say changes how anyone sees her. You've been carrying this for a long time. You deserve somewhere honest to set it down.
answer: That's a lot to carry, being both a student and your mum's main support. It's common to want to protect her reputation, but keeping things hidden can mean you're carrying the weight alone. Do you have a friend or mentor in the community you trust enough to share a small, real detail with? Sometimes just one person knowing the full picture can make a difference.

user: My boyfriend has bipolar disorder and we live together in Toronto. When he's manic he stops sleeping, makes impulsive decisions, and won't hear any concern. He says I'm trying to control him. Two years of this and I'm exhausted. I love him, but I feel like I'm the only thing between him and disaster.
gold: That feeling of being the only buffer is exhausting, and it's a sign that the system needs more support than you alone can give. When he's well, that's the time to have a conversation about what happens during manic episodes, before the next one. A written plan that he agrees to, who to call, when to involve his psych team, what you will and won't try to manage, can reduce the control dynamic. Does he have a care team you could connect with, with his permission? You're his partner, not his safety net, and you shouldn't have to hold this alone.
answer:
Two years of being the only one holding things together is exhausting, and it's not control to want someone you love to be safe. When he's manic, he's not thinking clearly, and it's not about you. It's about the illness.

Toronto has a range of resources for partners of people with bipolar disorder. The Canadian Mental Health Association has a local branch with support groups and education. And the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) has a family education program.

Does he have a psychiatrist? If so, you could ask to be part of his care team. If not, there are ways to get a referral. You're not alone in this, and you deserve support too.

user: I'm a fine arts student in Cape Town, Indigenous, and my younger brother's been on dialysis for over five years. We live together. Every resource I find is for parents or medical professionals, nothing for a sibling who's been doing this since basically a teenager.

Here's a couple of things that might help:

It's also important to remember that you're a student and an artist, not just a caregiver. Make sure you're carving out time for your own interests and well-being. If you're feeling overwhelmed, don't hesitate to reach out to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor for support.

user: My close friend has heart failure and moved in with me about a year ago. She keeps eating foods her cardiologist said to avoid, salty stuff, fast food. When I say anything she gets defensive and says I'm not her mother. I'm studying education in the US and I believe in respecting people's choices, but I'm watching her damage herself.
gold: That's a painful position, caring about someone's health while respecting their autonomy, and watching them make choices that worry you. She may be using food as one of the few things she still controls. Rather than monitoring what she eats, try shifting to: 'I'm not going to police your food, but I'm scared of losing you, can we talk about that?' It names your feeling without making her defensive. Her care team can also discuss diet in a way that feels less personal than hearing it from a friend. You can care without becoming the food police.
answer: It's a hard spot to be in, watching someone you care about make choices that seem harmful, especially when they're already dealing with a serious health condition. You're right to feel conflicted between respecting her autonomy and wanting to protect her. Her defensiveness is a sign of feeling controlled, and it's understandable she'd push back. You've already tried direct feedback, which can feel like nagging, even if it's well-intentioned. Maybe try asking her what would help her stick to her diet, or if she'd be open to a visit with a nutritionist who could help her find ways to enjoy food within her restrictions. If she's open to it, you could offer to cook meals together that fit her plan. If she's not, you can focus on making sure your own meals are healthy and available, and let her make her own choices. You're not responsible for her health, but you can be a supportive friend.

user: My closest friend has been fighting cancer for as long as I can remember and I support her from a few hours away while working full-time in social work. I'm Muslim and I pray for her constantly, but some days I feel like I'm drowning in helplessness. I don't know how to keep being strong for her.
gold: Feeling helpless when someone you love is fighting a long illness is one of the most painful parts of caring, and 'being strong' all the time isn't sustainable or fair to ask of yourself. Your prayers matter, and so do practical things: set a fixed call time so you're not both reaching out unpredictably, and ask if she'd share her nurse's contact with you so you have a source of information beyond what she feels able to share. And if there's an imam or a Muslim carer support group near you, that could be a space where faith and caregiving meet, where you don't have to explain either.
answer:
It's a lot to carry, being a distance away and working in a helping profession while your friend is in a long fight. Prayer is a lifeline, but it doesn't erase the helplessness. You're allowed to feel that, and it doesn't mean you're not strong.

Can you name one small thing you can do this week that's not about fixing anything, just being *with* her experience? A card, a scheduled phone call, a shared playlist? Sometimes the smallest gestures are the most sustaining.

If you're feeling overwhelmed, your employer may have an employee assistance program that offers counseling. And if you're able, a session with a therapist yourself can help you process the weight of this without feeling like you're taking away from your friend's space.

user: I'm a Hindu East Asian guy in Lagos, working part-time in biology. My younger sibling is on dialysis for kidney failure, about a year now. I use a shared Google Calendar for dialysis sessions and a WhatsApp group with his care team. It works but the WhatsApp group is so noisy I miss important updates from doctors.
gold: A shared calendar for dialysis sessions plus a WhatsApp group with the care team is a well-connected setup, and a year of that from a distance shows real dedication. The noise problem is common when clinical and casual messages mix in one group. A couple of things: could you ask the care team to prefix urgent messages with something like 'IMPORTANT' so they're scannable? Or would a separate thread, just you and the lead nurse, be possible for critical updates? And does your sibling's hospital offer a patient portal where results and appointment changes appear automatically? That could replace some of the WhatsApp scanning entirely.
answer: Noisy WhatsApp groups are a common problem in caregiving, and it's good you're noticing it's affecting your ability to get important updates. A dedicated care app might help, but if you're already using Google Calendar, you can try adding the care team to the calendar events and setting up email notifications for updates. And does your cousin know you keep the notes, and is she comfortable with it? If she's in the loop, it stays collaboration rather than surveillance. If not, that's worth a conversation. answer: It's good you're keeping notes, but you're right to question the line between tracking and over-monitoring. Focus on changes from her baseline, not just the symptoms themselves. For example, note if she's more withdrawn than usual, or if her sleep is disrupted, not just that she's experiencing paranoia. And medication changes are always worth noting, along with any side effects she reports. If you're still unsure, ask her psychiatrist what they'd find most helpful to know.

That's a really common feeling when someone you care about is diagnosed with something serious, and especially when you're long-distance. "Useless" is a strong word, and it's likely not true. It's more that you haven't yet found the right way to be helpful.

Genetic illnesses often have specific support groups, and those are a good place to start. They can offer practical advice, emotional support, and sometimes even financial assistance. You can also ask his family what they need, and be clear about what you can offer. Sometimes just being a listening ear is enough.

There are a few resources that might help:

*   **Rare Diseases International:** [https://www.rarediseases.org/](https://www.rarediseases.org/)
*   **Genetic Alliance:** [https://geneticalliance.org/](https://geneticalliance.org/)

And remember, it's okay to ask him directly what he needs from you. Sometimes the best support is simply being there to listen and validate his feelings.

gold: Being edited out of someone's reality, especially a partner's, is a particular kind of loneliness. After a stroke, minimising struggles often comes from wanting to feel normal or not wanting to be seen as vulnerable, even with someone who loves them. A practical approach: instead of asking 'how are you really?', try sharing something honest yourself first, 'today was hard for me too', which can make it safer for him to drop the front. And if he's working with a rehab team, they may have insight into whether this is a pattern they're seeing. You don't have to break through on your own.
answer:
It's a common pattern for people recovering from stroke to minimise their difficulties, often to protect those they love. It's a way of signalling independence, but it can be isolating for those around them. You're right to notice this, and it's understandable that you feel excluded.

Try asking him about specific things, not just 'how he is'. 'How's your speech therapy going?' or 'Are you still struggling with fatigue?' are less open to a simple 'fine' answer. You could also share your own feelings: 'I notice you say you're okay, but I worry when I hear that, because I know it's been hard.'

It's okay to ask him to be honest, and to say that you want to know the whole picture, even the hard parts. If he's reluctant, consider asking his care team if they can help you understand what's going on.

You're doing a great job supporting him from a distance, but it's important to remember that you can't do everything. If you're worried about his medication, talk to his doctor. Have you tried a brief check-in with yourself before opening the calendar or notes app, like naming one thing you're grateful for in your friend's life? If that doesn't help, maybe a different format for symptom tracking would feel lighter—a quick voice memo instead of typing, or a simple mood scale. If the heaviness persists, it might be worth talking to a counselor or support group for caregivers. They can help you sort out whether it's the system, you, or both.

user: I'm 18, a computer science apprentice in Mexico. My mum has heart failure and lives with me. It's only been a few months but I feel like I've lost my mum and gained a patient. She's not the same person. I'm agnostic so I don't have faith to lean on. I just feel empty and lost.
gold: That shift from having a mum to having someone you care for is one of the hardest transitions, and feeling empty and lost so early in this is completely understandable. It's a loss even though she's still here. You don't need faith to get through this. You need support. Two things: talk to your apprenticeship programme about what's happening at home. They may offer flexibility or connect you with counselling. And if there's a heart failure or cardiac support organisation in your area, they often have resources for family carers, including ones new to it. A counsellor could also help you process the grief of this role change. You're adjusting to a lot very quickly.
answer:
That's a really hard shift, losing the person you knew while still having them physically present. It's not just the loss of a mum, it's the loss of a future you imagined, and a grief that doesn't fit the usual timelines. Agnostic or not, it's okay to grieve the loss of the relationship you had, and to feel empty when the person you relied on for emotional support is no longer able to provide that.

It's okay to feel both grief and resentment, and to not have a neat answer for what you're feeling. It's okay to ask for help, even if it's just someone to talk to. Are there any support groups for carers in Mexico? Sometimes hearing other people's experiences can help you feel less alone.

user: I'm 21, a medical student in Mexico City. My grandfather is in another city with long COVID. I've been his distance carer essentially my whole life in some form. gold: Having the medical knowledge and still being dismissed as a family member rather than a colleague is uniquely maddening. Two practical things: put your concerns in writing, a concise, dated summary of his symptoms and what you'd like investigated, and ask his doctor to add it to his file. Written requests are harder to dismiss than verbal ones. And if possible, join his next appointment by phone or video so you can ask questions directly. As a medical student, your observations are valuable, but framing matters, lead with 'as his grandson who's also studying medicine' rather than just one or the other.
answer:
It's maddening to have the knowledge and still be dismissed. That's a very specific frustration, and it's valid. It's also a pattern that many carers, especially those with medical training, experience. It's not about your knowledge being wrong, it's about the system being rigid.

You've been his distance carer for a long time, and that's a lot of responsibility. It's okay to feel angry. It's okay to feel helpless. It's okay to feel like you're banging your head against a wall.

What's one small thing you can do to shift the power dynamic with his doctors? A written list of symptoms, a second opinion, a patient advocate? You don't have to do it all at once. And it's okay to ask for help.

user: I'm studying law and working part-time here in Jakarta. My older sibling is autistic and lives back home with our parents. For two years I've been sending money and calling every day. My Buddhist meditation group helps me manage stress, but I feel like I'm parenting from another country.
gold: Daily calls and financial support from another country is a substantial commitment, and 'parenting from a distance' is exactly how many long-distance carers describe it. Your meditation group helping with stress is genuinely valuable. A couple of practical thoughts: could you reduce the daily call to every other day, or shorten it, if the current pattern is draining you? And is there a trusted person near your sibling, a parent, a relative, who can be the primary eyes and ears so you're not the sole coordinator? It's okay to be one part of a support network rather than the whole thing.
answer:
Parenting from a distance is a unique kind of strain. It's not just the financial strain, but the emotional one of being unable to step in and help directly. It's good that you've found a meditation group that helps, but you're right to recognize that it's not enough.

You're in a situation where your parents are the primary caregivers, but you're also a key part of the care team. That means you need to be able to talk to your parents about what's working and what's not, and to set boundaries about what you can and can't do.

Here are some small steps:

*   **Schedule a regular family meeting:** A weekly call where you can all talk about your sibling's care.
*   **Talk to your parents about their needs:** What support do they need that you can provide?
*   **Set boundaries:** Be clear about how much money you can send and how often you can call.

You're doing a lot, and you're not alone. There are resources available to help you and your family. Here are a few:

*   **Autism Speaks:** [https://www.autismspeaks.org/](https://www.autismspeaks.org/)
*   **The Autism Society:** [https://www.autism-society.org/](https://www.autism-society.org/)
*   **National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI):** [https://www.nami.org/](https://www.nami.org/)

It's okay to ask for help, and it's okay to take care of yourself. You're a good sibling, and you're doing the best you can.

user: Mum had a spinal cord injury a few months ago and I live with her in Sydney. I work full-time in history research but since the injury I've basically become her carer. I haven't asked for any help yet and I don't know what I'm entitled to or where to look.
gold: A few months in, you're probably still in survival mode, and that's exactly when most people don't ask, because just getting through each day feels like enough. Can I ask: do you know if your mum has been assigned a social worker or care coordinator through her rehab or hospital? That person is often the gateway to home support services and carer payments. And separately, have you looked at Carers NSW? They specifically support young carers and can walk you through what's available. If you can tell me what your biggest daily struggle is, I can help you prioritise who to contact first.
answer:
It's understandable you haven't asked for help yet, many carers don't. You've stepped into a huge role alongside your work, and it's okay to acknowledge that's unsustainable.

The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is the main source of funding for disability support in Australia. Your mum's injury would likely qualify her, and you as her carer may be eligible for support too. The NDIS website has a good eligibility checker and information about accessing the scheme.

Carer Gateway is a national service that provides information, advice and support for carers. They can help you understand your rights, access respite care, and connect with other carers.

There are also local carer support services in Sydney. A good place to start is Carers NSW. They can offer counselling, peer support groups, and practical advice.

It's okay to ask for help. It doesn't mean you're failing as a daughter or as a carer. It means you're recognising your limits and prioritising both your mum's wellbeing and your own.

user: I'm 20, studying law and working part-time. My uncle moved in with us after developing long COVID. I've been his carer basically my whole life in different ways. As a Sikh, seva is central to who I am, but I'm falling behind in school and I feel trapped between duty and my future.
gold: Seva is a beautiful guiding principle, and it's also true that serving well requires you to not collapse under the weight of it, your future matters too. Two things that might help: talk to your university's disability or student support office about carer accommodations, many have flexible deadlines or note-taking support you may not know about. And check if your uncle qualifies for home support hours through your local health authority, even a few hours of outside help per week can protect your study time. Honouring seva doesn't mean doing it alone.
answer: It's a lot to carry, being a carer and a student. Seva is a beautiful value, but it's okay to admit that it's not sustainable to do it at the expense of your own wellbeing. Your future is important too. Have you talked to your family about getting some professional help for your uncle, even for a few hours a week? Or could you talk to your university about deferring a semester? It's not a failure to ask for help, it's a way of protecting your seva and your future.

user: Things are okay right now. I'm 25, recently graduated and job-seeking in graphic design, living in Ireland. I've cared for my mum who has epilepsy for three years, we live together. My Buddhist practice helps me stay grounded. Just wanted to check in.
gold: That's genuinely good to hear. Three years of co-resident care while studying and now job-seeking is a lot to hold, so a stable patch is worth appreciating. Since things are calm, this could be a good time to focus on your own base: is there something you've been putting off, a health check, catching up with friends, or just rest? Job-seeking alongside caregiving can blur into constant 'on' time, so protecting clear downtime matters. It can also help to note down what's working in your current routine, in case things shift.
answer: That's good to hear things are okay right now. Three years of caregiving is a long time, and finishing your degree on top of that is a lot. It's smart to keep checking in with yourself, and it's good your practice is a grounding force. Job-seeking is a full-time job in itself, so don't underestimate the energy that takes. If you want to talk about either the job hunt or the caregiving, or both, I'm here. Otherwise, just keep doing what you're doing.

user: My dad had a traumatic brain injury about a year ago. I'm 19, working full-time in India, and he's back home with my mum. I send money and call every day but I feel completely disconnected from what's actually happening with his recovery. I don't know what support I should even be looking for.
gold: Sending money and checking in daily from a distance is real, meaningful care, don't underestimate that. Two practical steps: ask your mum if you can speak briefly with your dad's doctor or rehab team, even by phone, so you understand his recovery trajectory rather than guessing. And look into TBI family support groups online, the Brain Injury Association has resources specifically for family members. Understanding what's happening will help you feel less in the dark and more useful.
answer: That disconnect is really common when you're far away, and it's a lot to carry on top of working full-time. You're right to ask about support, because it's not just about money. Is there a family friend or relative who can visit regularly and give you a detailed update after each visit? If your dad's recovery is being managed by a hospital or rehab centre, can they include you on email updates or phone calls? You could also look for TBI support groups online, even if they're not specific to India, just to hear how other families manage long-distance care. It's okay to ask for more than just financial help, and it's okay to feel lost about what that looks like.

user: My uncle in another city was diagnosed with diabetes complications a few months ago. I'm in Egypt working part-time in education and I'm agnostic. I want to help but I don't know what support services exist for distance carers here, or even what questions to ask.
gold: Wanting to help from a distance when it's all new shows real care, and not knowing what to ask is where everyone starts. Let me understand your situation a bit more. Are you the only person supporting your uncle, or are there other family members involved? And what does his current care setup look like, does he have a doctor he sees regularly, or is that something you're trying to help organise? Knowing this will help me point you toward the right kind of support.
answer:
It's good you're thinking ahead. Distance caregiving is a different beast, and Egypt's systems may not have the same resources as where your uncle is. Start by asking your uncle what he needs, and what he's already got covered. Then, ask his doctor if there's a care coordinator who can help with the practical side.

For distance carers, look for support groups online, even international ones. They can offer advice and a sense of community. If your uncle's complications affect his mobility, ask about home healthcare options. If he's struggling with the emotional side, suggest a counsellor or therapist.

Finally, remember you can't do everything. Set boundaries, and don't be afraid to ask for help from other family members.

user: My younger brother has Down syndrome and lives with me here in Vietnam. I'm studying graphic design part-time and I'm Hindu, my faith is very important to me. It's been about six months. He's started refusing to go to school, saying the other kids laugh at him. I don't know if I should make him go or let him stay home.
gold: That's a painful situation. He's telling you something real, and you're caught between protecting him and keeping his routine going. Refusing school when you're being laughed at isn't stubbornness, it's self-protection. Before deciding, talk to his school. They need to know what's happening, and many schools have inclusion policies they should be acting on. If the environment isn't safe, a different setting might serve him better. His paediatrician or a local disability organisation can also advise. Can I ask, does he open up about what specifically happens at school? That might help figure out the next step.
answer:
Six months is a long time to be figuring out a new rhythm, and it's especially hard when it involves someone else's wellbeing. It's good you're thinking about what's behind the refusal, not just the refusal itself. It's also good you're thinking about whether to push or allow, because both have consequences.

A refusal to go to school can be a sign of something deeper, and kids with Down syndrome are often very sensitive to social cues. If he's being laughed at, that's a real problem. But if he stays home, he'll miss out on learning and socialising.

I'm not sure what the school's policy is, or what kind of support they offer. It's worth talking to the teachers and the school counsellor to see what they say. If the school isn't supportive, you might need to look for another school.

In the meantime, maybe you could try talking to your brother about what's happening at school. Ask him what the other kids are saying, and how it makes him feel. If he's willing, you could role-play some ways to respond to the laughter.

And if you're feeling overwhelmed, don't be afraid to ask for help from your family or friends. You're not alone in this.

user: I'm a fine arts student in Lagos and my aunt with diabetes complications lives with us. I've been helping care for her as long as I can remember. gold: That triple mismatch, Western diet advice, Nigerian food, and Hindu dietary practice, makes most standard diabetes content genuinely useless for you. The Diabetes Association of Nigeria publishes localised dietary resources that account for Nigerian staples, and the International Diabetes Federation's Africa region has culturally adapted materials. For the Hindu dietary dimension, the Hindu American Association's health section sometimes addresses diabetes within vegetarian frameworks, and a dietitian at your aunt's clinic who understands both Nigerian and Hindu food practices could bridge the gap. Would asking her doctor for a referral to such a dietitian be possible?
answer: That's a really common problem, and it's so frustrating when information doesn't fit your life. You're right to notice that Western advice doesn't translate directly. Look for local diabetes educators or dietitians who work with Nigerian patients. They'll understand the food and cultural context. Also, ask your aunt's doctor if they can connect you with someone who has experience with both diabetes and the local diet. You're not alone in needing this kind of tailored support.

user: My cousin has Down syndrome and has lived with us in Amsterdam since forever. I study economics and work part-time. I use a family WhatsApp group to coordinate his care and a printed weekly rota on the wall. Lately people aren't checking the rota.
gold: A printed rota is a clear, visible system, the problem isn't the tool, it's that people stop looking at it when life gets busy. Before changing anything, it's worth asking: is the rota too detailed to scan quickly, or is the issue that people rely on the WhatsApp group instead and treat the rota as backup? If WhatsApp is where people actually look, it might be worth posting a weekly photo of the rota there every Sunday evening so it lands where attention already is. Sometimes the fix is meeting people where they already are.
answer:
That's frustrating. A rota that's not checked is a rota that's not working. It's a lot of work to keep a family care system running, and it's easy to feel like you're doing it all yourself when others don't follow through.

Can you ask the group to confirm they've seen the rota, and ask what would make it easier for them to check it? Maybe a daily reminder on WhatsApp? Or a digital rota that everyone can see?

user: My grandfather had a spinal cord injury a few months ago. I'm in Sweden studying psychology part-time, Christian background, and we're far apart. I'd be open to online support but only if it's practical and not just emotional sharing.
gold: That preference for practical focus is fair, some people want emotional sharing and others want concrete information, and mixing the two can feel frustrating. Look for spinal cord injury organisations that run online groups with a structured or educational format, some host sessions with rehab professionals or focus on specific topics like equipment, home adaptations, or navigating healthcare. Spinal cord injury charities in Scandinavia may offer online resources for family members. A group with a practical agenda alongside peer support might give you what you're after without the emotional sharing feeling forced.
answer:
Practical support for a spinal cord injury from a distance is about information, advocacy, and small tasks. Here's a breakdown:

*   **Information:** Spinal cord injuries vary hugely. Learn the specifics of his injury (complete/incomplete, level). The Swedish Spinal Cord Injury Association ([https://ryggmargsforeningen.se/en/](https://ryggmargsforeningen.se/en/)) has resources.
*   **Advocacy:** Ask his care team what you can do to help with paperwork, insurance, or equipment requests.
*   **Small Tasks:** Online bill pay, researching local services, coordinating visits, or just being a regular call to check on practical needs.
*   **Online Support:** The Spinal Cord Injury Association has online forums.

Focus on what you *can* do, even small things. It's okay to ask his care team for a list of specific needs.

user: I'm 18, a psychology student in Poland, and my mum was diagnosed with MS about a year ago. We live together and I'm her main carer. I'm not religious. I want to find support but I don't even know what exists for someone my age in this country.
gold: Being 18 and the main carer for your parent is a lot of responsibility to take on at the start of adulthood, and wanting support is the right instinct. And are you looking for practical help, things like someone to cover while you're at college, or more for emotional support and someone to talk to about the weight of it?
answer:
You're a psychology student, so you know the value of support, but it's different when you're *living* it. And you're doing this while studying, which is a huge amount to hold. It's really smart to look for help, and it's okay to not know where to start.

In Poland, the Polish Multiple Sclerosis Society (Polskie Towarzystwo Stwardnienia Rozsianego) has local branches that offer support groups and counselling. They sometimes have groups specifically for young carers. You can find them at [https://www.ptsms.pl/](https://www.ptsms.pl/) (the site is in Polish, so you might need a translator).

There's also a national carers' helpline, run by the Polish Carers' Association (Polskie Stowarzyszenie Rodzin Osób z Niepełnosprawnościami). It's called Telefon dla Osób Opiekujących and the number is 800 702 222.

You're not alone in this, and there are people who understand what you're going through. It's okay to ask for help, and it doesn't mean you're failing as a carer.

user: I've lived with and cared for my grandfather with Parkinson's for as long as I can remember. I'm 25 now, studying biology here in Dublin. You don't have to commit to anything, just observing others' experiences can tell you whether it's useful. And if there's a Parkinson's nurse specialist involved in your grandfather's care, they often know local resources for family carers. Worth a quiet ask.
answer: It's not unusual to feel like you're missing something when you've been caring for someone in isolation for a long time. You're right to wonder if connecting with other carers would add something to your routine. It's not about replacing your mum, or questioning your care, but about getting a space to talk with people who understand the specific challenges of caring. Parkinson's Ireland has a network of carers' groups, and they also run online forums. You could start there, and see if it feels right. It's okay to start small, even just reading posts, and see if it feels like a space where you could share your own experiences.

user: My uncle has Down syndrome and I've been caring for him from a distance in Indonesia for as long as I can remember. I'm an apprentice and my Sikh faith is central to my life. gold: The gap between what you're able to do from a distance and what you feel you should be doing is one of the most painful things about long-distance caregiving, and that sadness doesn't mean you're failing. And is there anyone physically near your uncle, a family member, a community worker, who you could coordinate with so you're not carrying the worry alone? Sometimes sharing the load with someone closer to him can ease that feeling of falling short.
answer:
It's not failing to feel sadness when distance keeps you from someone you love, especially when they need care. Your family's approach is practical, but it doesn't erase your need for closeness. Your Sikh faith likely values service and connection, and that longing is real.

Could you ask your family about a set time each week for a video call where you can simply *be* with your uncle, not just manage care? Or, if possible, could you plan a visit, even a short one, to reconnect physically? It's okay to ask for more than coordination, to ask for time to simply be his nephew.

user: I'm in Manila working part-time in psychology and my aunt with cystic fibrosis lives with me. I've been caring for two years. CF resources online are almost all American and focused on patients, not carers. The few carer things I find don't fit a niece's experience at all.
gold: That focus on patients over carers is a pattern in CF resources, and the niece role is almost never addressed specifically. The Cystic Fibrosis Worldwide network has a family section that's more inclusive of extended family than US-only sites, and the Philippine Society for Cystic Fibrosis (if active in your region) may have local carer connections. Your psychology background means you may also benefit from peer supervision groups where carer dynamics are understood. For practical day-to-day support, your aunt's respiratory team could connect you with other family carers. Would any of those feel worth exploring?
answer:
Two years is a long time to be caring, and it's not surprising that the resources aren't fitting. You're in a unique role, a niece, and in a different country, and the online world hasn't caught up with that. You're right to notice that gap.

You're also right to notice that most resources focus on the patient. That's the default, but it doesn't mean your experience isn't valid. You're not a patient, and you're not a parent, and that's a different set of needs.

If you're in Manila, there are a few things that might help. First, is there a local CF foundation or support group? Even if it's patient-focused, they might know of carer resources or be able to connect you with other carers. Second, is there a local psychology association that could offer carer support? Third, is there a local hospital that specializes in CF? They might have a social worker who could help you find resources.

If you can't find any local resources, you might try reaching out to a CF foundation in the US and asking if they have any resources for carers in other countries. They might not, but it's worth a try.

Finally, remember that you're not alone. There are other carers out there, even if they're not in Manila. You can find them online or through local support groups. And if you're feeling overwhelmed, don't hesitate to reach out to a trusted adult or professional for help.

user: My boyfriend is going through cancer treatment and lives with me here in London. I'm working part-time and it's been about six months. My Jewish community has been kind.
